Used before 1521: Chimalman, legendary woman who led the Mexica migration from Aztlan (also told of as a divine mother); written Chīmalmā (Chimalman). Chimalma is the Classical form without the final n. Some details are uncertain. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / Codex Chimalpahin)
A Classical Nahuatl word (citlalin, star), used as a given name today; no person of this name is recorded before 1521. Citlali is a modern given-name spelling of citlalin. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)
twisted grass; a day sign of the ritual calendar

A Classical Nahuatl word (malinalli, twisted grass; a day sign of the ritual calendar), used as a given name today; no person of this name is recorded before 1521. Malinali is a modern spelling of malinalli. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)
The name of the Maya (Yucatec) goddess Ix Chel, used as a given name today; not recorded as a woman's name before 1521. (Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán)
The name of the Nahua goddess Xīlōnen, used as a given name today; not recorded as a woman's name before 1521. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)
The name of the Maya (K'iche') goddess Awilix (Auilix), used as a given name today; not recorded as a woman's name before 1521. (Popol Vuh, tr. Allen J. Christenson)
crocodile (short for cipactli, a day sign)

Used before 1521: men and some women recorded in Mexico City, Cuernavaca, Tepetlaoztoc and Huexotzinco records, 16th century (usually male). Some details are uncertain. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: K'inich Janaab Pakal, ruler of Palenque, 603-683; written Pakal (K'inich Janahb' Pakal). (Mesoweb, Table of Palenque Rulers)

Used before 1521: Tizoc, seventh ruler of Tenochtitlan, r. 1481-1486; written Tizocic (Tizocicatzin). Tizoc is the usual short English form of Tizocic. (Visual Lexicon of Aztec Hieroglyphs, Tizocic / Codex Mendoza f.12r)

Used before 1521: Tenoch, legendary founder of Tenochtitlan (Codex Mendoza f.2r); also a man in the Morelos censuses, c.1540. Some details are uncertain. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes / Visual Lexicon)
Used before 1521: men recorded in the Morelos censuses, c.1540; written Quetzal (Quezall). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
warmth of the sun; day, fate
Used before 1521: men recorded in the Morelos censuses, c.1540; written Tonal (Donal). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: Tariácuri, founder of the Purépecha state, early 15th century. Tariacuri drops the accent of Tariácuri. (Relación de Michoacán, c.1539-41)
Used before 1521: Hiripan, nephew of Tariácuri, ruler (cazonci) d. c.1435. (Relación de Michoacán, c.1539-41)
Used before 1521: Zuangua, cazonci of the Purépecha, d. 1520. (Relación de Michoacán, c.1539-41)

Used before 1521: Miahuaxihuitl of Cuauhnahuac, queen of Tenochtitlan, mother of Motecuhzoma I, late 14th century; written Miahuaxihuitl (Miyahuaxihuitl). Miahua is a modern short form of Miahuaxihuitl. Some details are uncertain. (Chimalpahin / Online Nahuatl Dictionary)
Used before 1521: women recorded in the Morelos censuses, c.1540 (a birth-order name, common for girls); written Tlaco (Thlacv). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: women recorded in the Morelos censuses, c.1540; written Xoco (Xocv). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: wives recorded in the Morelos censuses, c.1540 (very common); written Necahual (Necaval). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: an unbaptized woman and others in the Morelos censuses, c.1540; written Centehua (Zeteva). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: Papanton, wife of Tezcacoacatl, Morelos censuses, c.1540; written Papanton (Papato). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)

Used before 1521: Ix Yohl Ik'nal, queen regnant of Palenque, r. 583-604. Yohl is one element of the attested name Ix Yohl Ik'nal, not a name on its own. Some details are uncertain. (Mesoweb, Table of Palenque Rulers)
Used before 1521: Ix Sak K'uk', mother of K'inich Janaab Pakal, d. 640. Sak Kuk is a modern spelling of Sak K'uk' without the glottal marks. (Mesoweb, Palenque dates)
Used before 1521: Ix K'abel, queen and Kaloomte' of Waka' (El Perú), 7th century. Kabel is a modern spelling of K'abel. Some details are uncertain. (Waka' Stela 34)
A Classical Nahuatl word (metztli, moon; month), used as a given name today; no person of this name is recorded before 1521. Metzli is a modern spelling of metztli. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)
The name of the Nahua goddess Mayahuel, used as a given name today; not recorded as a woman's name before 1521. (Codex Borgia / Florentine Codex)

Used before 1521: men and women of the 16th-century central Mexican records; also Xochitl, a Toltec noblewoman in Alva Ixtlilxochitl's chronicle; written Xōchitl (Xochitl, Suchitl). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)

Used before 1521: men and women of the 16th-century central Mexican records; also Xochitl, a Toltec noblewoman in Alva Ixtlilxochitl's chronicle; written Xōchitl. Xochi is a modern short form of Xochitl. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)

Used before 1521: an element in the names of K'inich Kan Bahlam II of Palenque (635-702) and Itzamnaaj Bahlam III of Yaxchilan (r. 681-742); written Bahlam (K'inich Kan B'ahlam; Itzamnaaj Bahlam). Balam is a modern spelling of Bahlam, a name element. (Mesoweb, Table of Palenque Rulers)
Used before 1521: Martín Ocelotl, Texcoco native priest tried by the Inquisition in 1536-37. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)

Used before 1521: Toribio Hacat, a household head; also children named Acatl, Morelos records c.1540; written Acatl (Hacat). Some details are uncertain. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: men named Mazatl in 16th-century records (Lockhart). (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)
Used before 1521: men recorded in the Morelos censuses, c.1540. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary / The Book of Tributes)
Used before 1521: men in the Matrícula de Huexotzinco, 1560; written Itzcuin (Cuin, Cuintli). Some details are uncertain. (Online Nahuatl Dictionary)

Used before 1521: Tangáxuan I, co-ruler with Hiripan, 15th century; Tzintzicha Tangaxuan II, last cazonci, r. 1520-1530; written Tangáxuan (Tzintzicha Tangaxuan). Tangaxuan drops the accent; x sounds like sh. (Relación de Michoacán, c.1539-41)
Used before 1521: Hiquíngare, son of Tariácuri, 15th century; written Hiquíngare (Hiquíngaje). Some details are uncertain. (Relación de Michoacán, c.1539-41)
